description.narrative: A MSc thesis has been written by Sophie Verheugd on the use of a numerical weather forecast model (WRF) to forecast rainfall up to ten days in advance. This should support decidion making at the beginning of the rainy season. Specifically, the question we want to be able to answer is if rainfall can be expected within the next 10 days to de-risk sowing. It often happens that no rains fall in the weeks after sowing, wasting the seed. The benchmark was the predictions made by the European Centre for Mid-range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). WRF was better at predicting rainfall but ECMWF was better at predicting days without rainfall. Next step is to use the TAHMO station to initialize WRF.

All weather stations in Ashanti, Bono and Ahafo, a total of 38, have been checked and upgraded as needed. Nine stations needed to be replaced. The heights of stations above sea level have now been carefully measured within 50cm. Earlier map-based heights differed up to 40m from the actual heights. This is important for the correction of the barometers. A 40m error can readily cause a numerical model to simulate wrongly a massive storm. All TAHMO barometers have also been calibrated with certified highly accurate barometers. This is the first step to be able to initiate numerical weather models properly. The problem with forecasts in Africa has to an important extent been that we don't know the present state of the atmosphere, so how can one predict tomorrow's state? There is no satellite substitute for barometric pressure and wind, which is what move air masses around.
Collins and FarmerLine continue to represent TAHMO and the project during the POMBI activities and gatherings.

Collins made a first round of interviewing twenty farmers about their information needs regarding the onset of the rainy season and present practices. They were very interested in having such information and also in possible insurance schemes for improved seeds. Selection of farmers has taken place in close cooperation with East-West Seed, which has also great interest in improved weather information. East-West Seed works more with poorer farmers who don't have access to irrigation (unlike HGT farmers) and depend on rainfall for germination. Improved seeds can triple a harvest but the costs are also very high. De-risking the sowing is, therefore, very relevant. This year was particularly poor in terms of rainfall, which may have skewed the discussions but also shows that the problem is very real. Next step will be a second round of half-structured interviews to understand in some detail what the value of onset information would be.
Overall: The network is now in good shape and we can start to run weather forecasts. The work with East-West Seed and WeatherImpact proceed well and awaits information from the farmers.

WeatherImpact continued analysis of onset information through ECMWF. ECMWF has two products, one up to two weeks and one up to 25 days. Both products give different results when it comes to the onset of the rainy season, also depending on the deginition of the onset. It is difficult to judge which is better until we have the information from the farmers on what information is crucial (see previous point).
